claim: Wdfy3 mRNA can be detected as early as embryonic day 11 (E11) in CNS tissue.
source: Multiplex, semi-quantitative RT-PCR revealed that Wdfy3 mRNA could be detected as early as embryonic day (E) 11 in CNS tissue, and remains detectable throughout gestation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Wdfy3 mRNA remains detectable throughout gestation.
source: Multiplex, semi-quantitative RT-PCR revealed that Wdfy3 mRNA could be detected as early as embryonic day (E) 11 in CNS tissue, and remains detectable throughout gestation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The highest concentration of Alfy is observed in the brain among adult tissues.
source: Similar analysis in adult tissue revealed that the Wdfy3 transcript is ubiquitously expressed, and that the highest concentration of Alfy was observed in the brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), confirming previous results (Simonsen et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and confirmed by previous citation

claim: Wdfy3 transcript is detected throughout both the perinatal and adult brain by in situ hybridization.
source: Wdfy3 transcript is detected throughout the both the perinatal and adult brain, as determined by in situ hybridization (ISH) (Figure 1B and not shown).
evidence: Supported by ISH experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Alfy protein is expressed uniformly throughout the brain.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that expression of the protein was present uniformly throughout the brain (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Endogenous Alfy expression is detected in both primary neuronal and purified astroglial cultures.
source: Using both primary neuronal and purified astroglial cultures, endogenous Alfy expression was detected in both cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), supporting recent transcriptome analysis of the mouse cortex (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cell culture data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and transcriptome analysis citation

claim: Alfy is a CNS-enriched protein present in various neuronal and non-neuronal cell types in the developing and adult brain.
source: Therefore, we conclude that Alfy is a CNS-enriched protein that is present in various neuronal and non-neuronal cell types in the developing and adult brain.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including RT-PCR, ISH, and immunoblotting data

claim: Homozygous Alfy GT mice are born at close to the expected Mendelian ratios.
source: Homozygous mice (Alfy GT) were born at close to the expected Mendelian ratios (WT: 19%, n = 20; Alfy GT Het: 52%, n = 54; Alfy GT: 28%, n= 29).
evidence: Supported by breeding data showing genotype ratios

claim: The full length Wdfy3 transcript is not produced in Alfy GT mice.
source: Primer pairs spanning the transcript indicated that the full length Wdfy3 transcript is not produced in Alfy GT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and antibodies directed against the NH3- or COOH-terminus of Alfy confirmed that full length Alfy protein was not detectable in brain lysates (not shown and Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and immunoblotting data

claim: Full length Alfy protein is not detectable in Alfy GT brain lysates.
source: Primer pairs spanning the transcript indicated that the full length Wdfy3 transcript is not produced in Alfy GT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and antibodies directed against the NH3- or COOH-terminus of Alfy confirmed that full length Alfy protein was not detectable in brain lysates (not shown and Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The GT insertion successfully mutagenized the Wdfy3 locus, leading to the loss of Alfy expression.
source: This demonstrates that the GT insertion successfully mutagenized the Wdfy3 locus, leading to the loss of Alfy expression.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RT-PCR and immunoblotting data showing absence of transcript and protein

claim: Alfy KO mice are born close to the expected Mendelian ratios.
source: Breeding of Wdfy3+/∆::HprtCre/+females with Wdfy3loxP/loxP::Hprt+/Y males generated mice heterozygous (Alfy Het) and homozygous (Alfy KO) for the null allele close to the expected Mendelian ratios (Alfy Het: 56%, n = 40; Alfy KO: 44%, n = 32).
evidence: Supported by breeding data showing genotype ratios

claim: Alfy protein is not detected in Alfy KO mice.
source: Alfy protein also was not detected in Alfy KO mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2D

claim: All neonatal Alfy mutant pups died several hours after birth.
source: Although neonatal Alfy mutant pups appeared grossly normal, were reactive, and showed no sign of cyanosis, they all died several hours after birth.
evidence: Observation of perinatal lethality in Alfy mutant mice

claim: Alfy mutant pups failed to thrive and consistently showed an absence of milk in their stomachs.
source: Unlike their littermates, Alfy mutant pups failed to thrive and consistently showed an absence of milk in their stomachs (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by observational data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Alfy mutant pups were frequently the smallest pups within the litter.
source: Despite being properly cleaned, live Alfy mutant pups were frequently the smallest pups within the litter (Figure 2F) and were selectively buried under nesting material, indicating that the dams were rejecting them due to diminished or uncoordinated movement (Turgeon and Meloche, 2009).
evidence: Supported by birth weight data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Dams were rejecting Alfy mutant pups due to diminished or uncoordinated movement.
source: Despite being properly cleaned, live Alfy mutant pups were frequently the smallest pups within the litter (Figure 2F) and were selectively buried under nesting material, indicating that the dams were rejecting them due to diminished or uncoordinated movement (Turgeon and Meloche, 2009).
evidence: Inference based on observed behavior and supported by citation

claim: Mice lacking Alfy consistently failed the righting reflex test.
source: Littermates with at least one copy of Alfy were able to right themselves within the allotted test time. In contrast, mice lacking Alfy consistently failed at this test, and demonstrated uncoordinated behavior.
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Mice lacking Alfy demonstrated uncoordinated behavior.
source: Littermates with at least one copy of Alfy were able to right themselves within the allotted test time. In contrast, mice lacking Alfy consistently failed at this test, and demonstrated uncoordinated behavior.
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Brains from Alfy GT and Alfy KO demonstrated striking abnormalities in the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.
source: Histological examination of the newborn (P0) brain by Nissl staining revealed that brains from Alfy GT and Alfy KO both demonstrated striking abnormalities in the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain, including visibly smaller brains and gross enlargement of the lateral ventricles (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Alfy mutant brains have visibly smaller brains and gross enlargement of the lateral ventricles.
source: Histological examination of the newborn (P0) brain by Nissl staining revealed that brains from Alfy GT and Alfy KO both demonstrated striking abnormalities in the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain, including visibly smaller brains and gross enlargement of the lateral ventricles (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: There was an apparent loss and disorganization of interhemispheric axonal tracts throughout the Alfy mutant brain.
source: Concurrently, there was an apparent loss and disorganization of interhemispheric axonal tracts throughout the brain.
evidence: Observation from histological examination

claim: Brains of Alfy GT Het or Alfy Het mice were indistinguishable from wildtype brains.
source: Brains of Alfy GT Het or Alfy Het mice were indistinguishable from wildtype brains (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by histological comparison shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: NF labeling of Alfy null brains was greatly reduced, suggesting fewer axonal tracts.
source: When compared to control, NF labeling of Alfy null brains was greatly reduced, suggesting fewer axonal tracts.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data and inference from reduced labeling

claim: Axons of the corpus callosum, hippocampal commissure, and anterior commissure failed to decussate in Alfy null brains.
source: Axons of the corpus callosum, hippocampal commissure (Figure 3C), and anterior commissure (Figure 3D) failed to decussate, leading to a separation of the two hemispheres.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C,D

claim: The failure of commissures to decussate led to a separation of the two hemispheres in Alfy null brains.
source: Axons of the corpus callosum, hippocampal commissure (Figure 3C), and anterior commissure (Figure 3D) failed to decussate, leading to a separation of the two hemispheres.
evidence: Inference from observed commissure defects

claim: The habenular and posterior commissures were morphologically abnormal and reduced in size in Alfy null brains.
source: Two smaller, caudal commissures, the habenular and posterior commissures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), were morphologically abnormal and reduced in size however a portion of their tracts crossed the midline.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: A portion of the habenular and posterior commissure tracts crossed the midline in Alfy null brains.
source: Two smaller, caudal commissures, the habenular and posterior commissures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), were morphologically abnormal and reduced in size however a portion of their tracts crossed the midline.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The ipsilateral projection in Alfy GT mice at P0 was 40% larger than that in wildtype or heterozygous mice.
source: At P0, the ipsilateral projection in Alfy GT mice (1.40 ± 0.06) was 40% larger than that in wildtype (1.0 ± 0.08) or heterozygous mice (1.1 ± 0.06) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by DiI labeling and quantification data shown in Figure 4C

claim: In Alfy mutants, contralateral axons less readily cross the optic chiasm midline.
source: This significant difference suggests that in Alfy mutants, contralateral axons less readily cross the optic chiasm midline.
evidence: Inference from ipsilateral index data

claim: Alfy is required to properly establish commissures throughout the developing mouse brain.
source: These data reinforce the findings that Alfy is required to properly establish commissures throughout the developing mouse brain.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple commissure defect observations

claim: The indusium griseum cells were not detectable in Alfy GT brains.
source: In Alfy GT brains, the ig was not detectable (expected location denoted by '*'), and the gw and mz cells were disorganized.
evidence: Supported by GFAP immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The glial wedge and midline zipper cells were disorganized in Alfy GT brains.
source: In Alfy GT brains, the ig was not detectable (expected location denoted by '*'), and the gw and mz cells were disorganized.
evidence: Supported by GFAP immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Glial populations within the fimbria and dentate gyrus of the hippocampus were apparent in both Alfy GT and control genotypes.
source: Glial populations within the fimbria (fi) and dentate gyrus (dg) of the hippocampus were apparent in both genotypes.
evidence: Supported by GFAP immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Cells that act as important guideposts for decussating callosal axons fail to migrate properly in the absence of Alfy.
source: These findings suggest that cells that act as important guideposts for decussating callosal axons (Shu and Richards, 2001) fail to migrate properly in the absence of Alfy, contributing to the connectivity defects observed.
evidence: Inference from glial cell mislocalization data and supported by citation

claim: The cortical plate/subplate of Alfy GT brains are modestly but significantly thinner than control brains at P0.
source: Measurements of P0 cortex reveal that the cortical plate/subplate (CP/SP) of Alfy GT brains (n = 3) are modestly but significantly thinner than control (Ctrl, n = 3) brains, (t(4) = 5.30, p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by cortical thickness measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: There was a modest yet significant reduction in the number of BrdU-positive cells in Alfy KO embryos at E15.5.
source: No significant difference across genotypes was detected at E13.5, but a modest yet significant reduction in the number of BrdU-positive cells was detected in Alfy KO embryos at E15.5.
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling and quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: There were no detectable differences across genotypes in the amount of cell death in E15.5 brains.
source: Further, despite this modest decrease in embryonic proliferation, there were no detectable differences across genotypes in the amount of cell death in E15.5 brains, as indicated by immunohistochemistry against cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by cleaved caspase-3 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Focal cortical dysplasias are present throughout the cerebral cortex of Alfy KO mice.
source: Although qualitative immunofluorescence against expression markers for immature migrating neurons (DCX) and for early born layer VI neurons (Tbr1) also were not significantly altered in the absence of Alfy, histological staining revealed focal cortical malformations known as focal cortical dysplasias (FCD) present throughout the cerebral cortex of Alfy KO mice, as described previously in a Wdfy3 hypomorph (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E) (Orosco et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E and confirmed by previous citation

claim: Focal cortical dysplasias were observed as early as E15.5 in Alfy KO mice.
source: These structures were observed as early as E15.5.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E

claim: The internal capsule of Alfy GT brains was disorganized and followed an unusual trajectory through the striatum.
source: One particularly prominent defect was found in the organization of the internal capsule, which carries the corticospinal tract, and corticothalamic and thalamocortical projections; the internal capsule of Alfy GT brains was disorganized and followed an unusual trajectory through the striatum (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by NF staining data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The thalamocortical projections in Alfy GT mice formed ventrally displaced bundles at E15.5 and E17.5.
source: NF staining revealed the expected fasciculated axonal projections of the developing internal capsule en route to and from the cerebral cortex in controls. In contrast, the thalamocortical projections in Alfy GT mice formed ventrally displaced bundles, with fewer projections observed traveling through the ganglionic eminence.
evidence: Supported by NF staining data shown in Figure 5A,B

claim: Alfy GT embryonic brain sections labeled with NCAML1 highlighted abnormal bundle-like structures in the ventral diencephalic-telencephalic border.
source: Similarly, Alfy GT embryonic brain sections labeled with the axonal marker NCAML1 also highlighted abnormal bundle-like structures in the ventral diencephalic-telencephalic border (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by NCAML1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The A9 and A10 DAergic populations in Alfy GT brains revealed an immature appearance relative to control littermates at P0.
source: Notably, the A9 and A10 cell populations, which represent the ventral tegmental area (A9) and substantia nigra (A10), revealed that the morphology of the regions had an immature appearance relative to control littermates at the same age (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by TH staining data shown in Figure 5C

claim: In Alfy KO brain, ectopic TH fibers were observed projecting ventrolaterally into the hypothalamus, near the location of the supraoptic decussation.
source: Moreover, rather than follow their typical trajectory through the medium forebrain bundle to striatal targets in the forebrain, in Alfy KO brain, ectopic TH fibers were observed projecting ventrolaterally into the hypothalamus, near the location of the supraoptic decussation (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by TH staining data shown in Figure 5C,D

claim: Disorganized projections into gray matter and the loss of axon bundles were evident in the cervical, thoracic and lumbar levels of the spinal cord in the absence of Alfy at E13.5.
source: At E13.5, disorganized projections into gray matter and the loss of axon bundles were evident in the cervical, thoracic and lumbar levels of the spinal cord in the absence of Alfy, but not in control littermates (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by NF staining data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Alfy is essential for establishing axonal tracts throughout the CNS, from forebrain commissures to the spinal cord.
source: In summary, these data indicate that Alfy is essential for establishing axonal tracts throughout the CNS, from forebrain commissures to the spinal cord.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple observations of axonal defects throughout the CNS

claim: An abnormal dopaminergic commissure at the level of the diencephalon traveling through the hypothalamus from the MFB has been previously reported in the Slit1/Slit2 double KO.
source: For example, an abnormal dopaminergic commissure at the level of the diencephalon traveling through the hypothalamus from the MFB has been previously reported in the Slit1/Slit2 double KO (Bagri et al., 2002), the Deleted in colorectal cancer (Dcc) KO (Xu et al., 2010), and the NK2 Homeobox 1 (Nkx2.1) KO (Kawano et al., 2003) mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: An abnormal dopaminergic commissure at the level of the diencephalon traveling through the hypothalamus from the MFB has been previously reported in the Dcc KO.
source: For example, an abnormal dopaminergic commissure at the level of the diencephalon traveling through the hypothalamus from the MFB has been previously reported in the Slit1/Slit2 double KO (Bagri et al., 2002), the Deleted in colorectal cancer (Dcc) KO (Xu et al., 2010), and the NK2 Homeobox 1 (Nkx2.1) KO (Kawano et al., 2003) mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: An abnormal dopaminergic commissure at the level of the diencephalon traveling through the hypothalamus from the MFB has been previously reported in the Nkx2.1 KO.
source: For example, an abnormal dopaminergic commissure at the level of the diencephalon traveling through the hypothalamus from the MFB has been previously reported in the Slit1/Slit2 double KO (Bagri et al., 2002), the Deleted in colorectal cancer (Dcc) KO (Xu et al., 2010), and the NK2 Homeobox 1 (Nkx2.1) KO (Kawano et al., 2003) mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Alfy may be involved in the ability of neural cells to respond to guidance cues.
source: We therefore hypothesized that Alfy may be involved in the ability of neural cells to respond to guidance cues.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observed phenotypes and comparison to other guidance mutants

claim: Full length Alfy localizes throughout the neuron, including within the axon.
source: Full length Alfy constructs with an N-terminus tag were transfected into DIV7 dissociated primary cortical cultures. Alfy localized throughout the neuron, including within the axon.
evidence: Supported by transfection and imaging data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Neighboring astroglia showed a diffuse localization of Alfy.
source: Neighboring astroglia also showed a diffuse localization of Alfy (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by transfection and imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Alfy enriched in the light membrane fraction (P3) along with synaptophysin and LC3-II.
source: Fractionation revealed that Alfy enriched in the light membrane fraction (P3) along with synaptosomal membrane protein synaptophysin and a classic marker for autophagic vesicles, the membrane bound form of microtubule associated protein light chain 3 (LC3-II) (Kabeya et al., 2000) (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 6B,C and citation for LC3-II marker

claim: Alfy was enriched in the crude synaptic vesicle fraction (LP1).
source: Additionally, Alfy was enriched in the crude synaptic vesicle fraction (LP1).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 6B,C

claim: Alfy may be involved in regulating the trafficking, sorting or signaling events that are required for brain wiring.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Alfy may be involved in regulating the trafficking, sorting or signaling events that are required for brain wiring.
evidence: Inference from subcellular localization data

claim: Alfy KO neurons displayed healthy growth in vitro at DIV7.
source: Alfy KO neurons displayed healthy growth in vitro and Scholl analysis confirmed that they were morphologically similar to control (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Alfy KO neurons were morphologically similar to control neurons at DIV7.
source: Alfy KO neurons displayed healthy growth in vitro and Scholl analysis confirmed that they were morphologically similar to control (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by Scholl analysis data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Neuronal cytoskeletal markers Tau-1, βIII Tubulin and MAP2 were expressed comparably across genotypes.
source: Staining also revealed that the neuronal cytoskeletal markers Tau-1, βIII Tubulin and microtubule associated protein 2 (MAP2) were expressed comparably across genotypes (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining observations

claim: Alfy is not required for processes controlling non-directed neuronal outgrowth in a cell autonomous manner.
source: Taken together, these data indicate Alfy is not required for processes controlling non-directed neuronal outgrowth in a cell autonomous manner.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from morphological analysis of cultured neurons

claim: In the presence of Netrin-1, control explants demonstrate significantly increased growth.
source: In the presence of Netrin-1, control explants demonstrate significantly increased growth whereas Alfy KO explants did not respond, despite maintaining their ability to extend their processes under non-stimulated conditions (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by explant outgrowth assay data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Alfy KO explants did not respond to Netrin-1.
source: In the presence of Netrin-1, control explants demonstrate significantly increased growth whereas Alfy KO explants did not respond, despite maintaining their ability to extend their processes under non-stimulated conditions (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by explant outgrowth assay data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Alfy KO explants maintained their ability to extend their processes under non-stimulated conditions.
source: In the presence of Netrin-1, control explants demonstrate significantly increased growth whereas Alfy KO explants did not respond, despite maintaining their ability to extend their processes under non-stimulated conditions (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by explant outgrowth assay data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Alfy is required for cortical neurons to respond to the trophic effects of Netrin-1.
source: These data indicate that Alfy is required for cortical neurons to respond to the trophic effects of Netrin-1.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from explant outgrowth assay data

claim: The loss of Alfy did not affect the total levels of the guidance cue receptor DCC.
source: The loss of Alfy did not affect the total levels of the guidance cue receptor DCC (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C

claim: Alfy function could involve the regulation of intracellular membrane-based signaling events in response to changes in the extracellular milieu of the developing brain.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that Alfy function could involve the regulation of intracellular membrane-based signaling events in response to changes in the extracellular milieu of the developing brain.
evidence: Inference from guidance cue responsiveness data and receptor level data

claim: Alfy was an adaptor protein for the degradation of aggregated proteins by selective macroautophagy.
source: We and others previously found using stable cell lines that Alfy was an adaptor protein for the degradation of aggregated proteins by selective macroautophagy (Clausen et al., 2010; Filimonenko et al., 2010; Lystad et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Non-selective macroautophagy remains intact in tissues and cells derived from Alfy null mice.
source: Consistent with previous findings, non-selective macroautophagy remains intact in tissues and cells derived from Alfy null mice (Filimonenko et al., 2010) (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A–D and confirmed by previous citation

claim: Mice lacking Alfy clearly mounted an autophagic response to starvation as indicated by the increased levels of LC3-II in lysates collected from the perinatal liver.
source: Mice lacking Alfy clearly mounted an autophagic response to starvation as indicated by the increased levels of LC3-II in lysates collected from the perinatal liver (Figure 8A), which is consistent with the lack of feeding observed in the pups (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 8A

claim: No abnormal accumulation of LC3-II was observed in the Alfy null brain.
source: Although neurons can properly mount an autophagic response (Figure 8D), no abnormal accumulation of LC3-II was observed in the brain (Figure 8B), suggesting that autophagosome maturation also is unaffected.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Autophagosome maturation is unaffected in Alfy null brain.
source: Although neurons can properly mount an autophagic response (Figure 8D), no abnormal accumulation of LC3-II was observed in the brain (Figure 8B), suggesting that autophagosome maturation also is unaffected.
evidence: Inference from LC3-II levels in brain

claim: Macroautophagic degradation of long lived proteins was independent of Alfy expression.
source: Consistent with this finding, macroautophagic degradation of long lived proteins was also independent of Alfy expression (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by long lived protein degradation assay data shown in Figure 8C

claim: In the absence of Alfy, ubiquitinated ALIS structures accumulated more rapidly.
source: Cytosolic ubiquitinated ALIS were formed in MEFs upon mitotic inhibition (Figure 8E). In contrast to control MEFs, these structures accumulated more rapidly in the absence of Alfy, suggesting that in its absence, the turnover of ALIS are impeded.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8E

claim: In the absence of Alfy, the turnover of ALIS is impeded.
source: Cytosolic ubiquitinated ALIS were formed in MEFs upon mitotic inhibition (Figure 8E). In contrast to control MEFs, these structures accumulated more rapidly in the absence of Alfy, suggesting that in its absence, the turnover of ALIS are impeded.
evidence: Inference from ALIS accumulation data

claim: Alfy GT MEFs do not demonstrate basal protein accumulation.
source: Moreover, unlike in MEFs that lack all forms of macroautophagy (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) (Kuma et al., 2004), Alfy GT MEFs do not demonstrate basal protein accumulation, suggesting that Alfy is not required for the turnover of all ubiquitinated substrates.
evidence: Supported by comparison to Atg5 KO MEFs and citation

claim: Alfy is not required for the turnover of all ubiquitinated substrates.
source: Moreover, unlike in MEFs that lack all forms of macroautophagy (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) (Kuma et al., 2004), Alfy GT MEFs do not demonstrate basal protein accumulation, suggesting that Alfy is not required for the turnover of all ubiquitinated substrates.
evidence: Inference from lack of basal accumulation in Alfy GT MEFs

claim: Over-expression of 17aahtt(103Q)eGFP accumulated more rapidly in the absence of Alfy.
source: Nonetheless, over-expression of a canonical aggregation-prone polyQ protein, a 17 amino acid fragment of the mutant huntingtin protein with 103 glutamines and an eGFP tag (17aahtt(103Q)eGFP) (Kazantsev et al., 1999), accumulated more rapidly by the absence of Alfy (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by transfection and imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D and citation

claim: In the absence of Alfy, the elimination of ubiquitinated proteins by selective macroautophagy, but not basal macroautophagy, is impaired.
source: Thus, in the absence of Alfy, the elimination of ubiquitinated proteins by selective macroautophagy, but not basal macroautophagy, is impaired.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from ALIS and polyQ accumulation data

claim: Alfy-mediated sequestration of cargoes may help selectively eliminate cargoes at or around the membrane, thereby affecting the ability of axons to properly respond to guidance cues.
source: Taken together with the rest of our findings, we hypothesize that Alfy-mediated sequestration of cargoes may help selectively eliminate cargoes at or around the membrane, thereby affecting the ability of axons to properly respond to guidance cues.
evidence: Hypothesis based on integration of multiple experimental findings

claim: Alfy influences how growing axons interact with their environment to form stereotyped axonal connectivity in the central nervous system.
source: In this study, our genetic models revealed that Alfy influences how growing axons interact with their environment to form stereotyped axonal connectivity in the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations

claim: The homozygous loss of Wdfy3 disrupts the formation of many axonal connections, causing agenesis of all three forebrain commissural tracts.
source: The homozygous loss of Wdfy3 disrupts the formation of many axonal connections, causing agenesis of all three forebrain commissural tracts and leading to profound changes in brain wiring throughout the CNS, including the optic chiasm, internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, medial forebrain bundle and spinal cord tracts.
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental observations

claim: The loss of Alfy led to defects in the development of midline glial population.
source: At the cellular level, the loss of Alfy led to defects in the development of midline glial population, impacted embryonic cortical neuron proliferation and impeded the ability of axons to respond to Netrin-1.
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental observations

claim: The loss of Alfy impacted embryonic cortical neuron proliferation.
source: At the cellular level, the loss of Alfy led to defects in the development of midline glial population, impacted embryonic cortical neuron proliferation and impeded the ability of axons to respond to Netrin-1.
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental observations

claim: The loss of Alfy impeded the ability of axons to respond to Netrin-1.
source: At the cellular level, the loss of Alfy led to defects in the development of midline glial population, impacted embryonic cortical neuron proliferation and impeded the ability of axons to respond to Netrin-1.
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental observations

claim: Alfy KO mice present a phenotype unlike mice lacking core autophagy genes such as Atg5.
source: Furthermore, Alfy KO mice present a phenotype unlike mice lacking core autophagy genes such as Atg5, suggesting the perinatal lethality is not due to a loss of general autophagic degradation, as Alfy mutant tissue and cells display the classic response to starvation.
evidence: Comparison to other autophagy mutants and experimental observations

claim: The perinatal lethality in Alfy mutants is not due to a loss of general autophagic degradation.
source: Furthermore, Alfy KO mice present a phenotype unlike mice lacking core autophagy genes such as Atg5, suggesting the perinatal lethality is not due to a loss of general autophagic degradation, as Alfy mutant tissue and cells display the classic response to starvation.
evidence: Inference from comparison to other autophagy mutants and starvation response data

claim: Alfy functions as a selective macroautophagy adaptor protein.
source: We hypothesize that Alfy functions as a selective macroautophagy adaptor protein and that Alfy-dependent regulation of intracellular vesicle trafficking and signaling pathways upstream of macroautophagy can have a significant influence over brain development.
evidence: Hypothesis based on integration of experimental findings

claim: Alfy-dependent regulation of intracellular vesicle trafficking and signaling pathways upstream of macroautophagy can have a significant influence over brain development.
source: We hypothesize that Alfy functions as a selective macroautophagy adaptor protein and that Alfy-dependent regulation of intracellular vesicle trafficking and signaling pathways upstream of macroautophagy can have a significant influence over brain development.
evidence: Hypothesis based on integration of experimental findings

claim: APs are present in the growth cone and axon tips.
source: For instance, APs are present in the growth cone and axon tips (Hollenbeck, 1993; Maday and Holzbaur, 2014; Maday et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Alfy could regulate the ability of growth cones to respond to cues by sequestering and sorting proteins into degradative vesicles.
source: We propose that Alfy could regulate the ability of growth cones to respond to cues by sequestering and sorting proteins into degradative vesicles.
evidence: Hypothesis based on known Alfy function and growth cone biology

claim: The ubiquitination of guidance receptor complexes could regulate the responsiveness of axons to guidance cues.
source: It has been suggested previously that the ubiquitination of guidance receptor complexes could regulate the responsiveness of axons to guidance cues (O'Donnell et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The trafficking and responsiveness of the axonal guidance receptors Robo1 and UNC5 has been shown to be regulated by E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: The trafficking and responsiveness of the axonal guidance receptors Robo1 and UNC5 has been shown to be regulated by the E3 ubiquitin ligases rpm-1 in C. elegans and USP33 in murine commissural axons, respectively (Li et al., 2008; Yuasa-Kawada et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Deletion of the rpm-1 homologue, Phr1, in mice, causes axonal wiring defects reminiscent of Alfy mutants.
